intro: The Notturno, marked Andante, is the slow third movement of Borodin’s String Quartet No. 2 in D major. It is in A major, and the cello plays the main theme over a syncopated accompaniment. Wright and Forrest adapted that theme in 1953 for the musical Kismet.

sections.label: A · Cello theme over syncopated accompaniment
A · First violin, cello on long notes, letter A
A · Tempo I, cello theme returns
sections.mNote: The cello plays the theme again, marked fp cant. espressivo.

sections.label: Coda · Pizzicato, sustained notes, final statement

cues.title: Opening cello theme
cues.text: The cello plays the theme, marked solo and cantab. ed espressivo, in A major and 3/4, over a rocking syncopated accompaniment in the second violin and viola. The first violin rests. The cello part lies high, on ledger lines above the bass staff.
cues.evidence: Parts of the Belaieff first edition (Leipzig, 1888), Internet Archive item 31761034881623, Notturno, p. 7: cello, Andante, solo, cantab. ed espressivo; second violin and viola, syncopated figures from bar 1; first violin, rests with cue notes until letter A. Fanning’s note for CDA68166 describes a “rocking, syncopated accompaniment”: https://archive.org/details/31761034881623
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First violin at letter A
cues.text: At letter A the first violin enters high in its range, marked p cant. e espress., while the cello holds dotted minims marked p, one to a bar.
cues.evidence: Belaieff 1888 parts, Notturno, p. 7: first violin, rests with cue notes to bar 23, then p cant. e espress. at letter A; cello, letter A, dotted minims marked p.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Dedication to Ekaterina, 1881
cues.text: Borodin wrote the quartet in the summer of 1881 and dedicated it to his wife, Ekaterina. He had just returned from a German tour that included Heidelberg, where they had met in 1861.
cues.evidence: David Fanning, Hyperion note for CDA68166 (2017): composed summer 1881, dedicated to Borodin’s wife, after a German tour taking in Heidelberg, https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W333_68166. Meeting in Heidelberg in 1861: Russian Biographical Dictionary, vol. 3 (1908), “Borodin”, https://ru.wikisource.org/wiki/РБС/ВТ/Бородин,_Александр_Порфирьевич

cues.title: Faster central section
cues.text: At letter B the tempo changes to a tempo più mosso, with accents in the cello part. David Fanning’s note says the faster central section lets the second violin join in a dialogue on rising scales.
cues.evidence: Belaieff 1888 parts, Notturno, p. 7: a tempo più mosso at letter B in the cello part, accents; second violin, two bars’ rest with cue notes of the first violin, then rising scales marked appassionato e risoluto (p. 8). Fanning’s note on the faster central section: https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W333_68166
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Use in Kismet, 1953
cues.text: In 1953 Robert Wright and George Forrest used this movement’s main theme for the song “And This Is My Beloved” in Kismet. The second theme of the Scherzo became “Baubles, Bangles and Beads”.
cues.evidence: David Fanning, Hyperion note for CDA68166 (2017): the musical Kismet appropriated the Scherzo’s second theme and the Notturno’s main theme. https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W333_68166

cues.title: Letter C, cello cantabile
cues.text: At letter C the cello plays a cantabile line marked p. A crescendo follows, marked sempre cresc., through f risoluto to ff with trills.
cues.evidence: Cello part, Belaieff 1888, Notturno, p. 7: letter C, p cantab., sempre cresc., f risoluto, ff and trills.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the theme, cello
cues.text: At letter D the opening tempo returns and the cello plays the theme again, fp, marked cant. espressivo.
cues.evidence: Cello part, Belaieff 1888, Notturno, p. 8: Tempo I at letter D.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Cello pizzicato, letter E
cues.text: At letter E the cello plays pizzicato, marked mf, in repeated three-note figures that run for some twenty bars.
cues.evidence: Cello part, Belaieff 1888, Notturno, p. 8: letter E, pizz., mf, repeated three-note figures.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Cello arco at letter F
cues.text: At letter F the cello returns to the bow with held notes marked p, and the pizzicato figures stop.
cues.evidence: Cello part, Belaieff 1888, Notturno, p. 8: letter F, arco, p, dotted minims.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Final cello statement, letter G
cues.text: At letter G the cello rises in a last statement marked fp espress. e cantab.
cues.evidence: Cello part, Belaieff 1888, Notturno, p. 8: letter G, fp espress. e cantab.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Final bars
cues.text: The last phrase is marked dim. perdendosi, and the movement ends on a held note under a pause.
cues.evidence: Cello part, Belaieff 1888, Notturno, p. 8, last system: dim. perdendosi, final note with fermata.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

composer.epithet: Russian chemist, professor at the Medical-Surgical Academy in Saint Petersburg, who composed two symphonies, two string quartets and the opera Prince Igor.
facts: Medical-Surgical Academy, Saint Petersburg, 1850–58; chemistry under Nikolay Zinin; Heidelberg, 1859–61; guidance in composition from Mily Balakirev
Adjunct professor of chemistry at the Academy from 1862, professor from 1864; lecturer at the women’s medical courses from 1872
Balakirev · Mussorgsky · Cui · Rimsky-Korsakov · Stasov · Liszt at Weimar
Two symphonies and part of a third, Prince Igor (completed by others), two string quartets, In the Steppes of Central Asia, songs, piano music

quote.text: For me, it is a relaxation, a pastime which distracts me from my principal business, my professorship.
quote.source: Borodin to Lyudmila Karmalina, 10 June 1876, in Alfred Habets, Borodin and Liszt (trans. Rosa Newmarch)

composer.background:
Alexander Borodin was born in Saint Petersburg on 12 November 1833, which was 31 October in the Russian calendar of the day. His father, Luka Gedianov, was a Georgian prince, and his mother, Avdotya Antonova, a soldier’s daughter. As was usual in such cases, the boy was registered as the son of one of Gedianov’s serfs, Porfiry Borodin. He was taught at home. His first compositions were a flute concerto of 1847 and a trio for two violins and cello on a theme from Meyerbeer’s Robert le diable. With his friend Mikhail Shchiglev he played the symphonies of Haydn, Beethoven and Mendelssohn as piano duets, and he learnt the cello.

In 1850 Borodin entered the Medical-Surgical Academy, and from his third year he worked in the laboratory of the chemist Nikolay Zinin. Zinin named him as his successor and warned him in public that “you make a mistake in hunting two hares at once”. In the autumn of 1856, as a young army surgeon, Borodin met the seventeen-year-old guards officer Mussorgsky at a military hospital. He took his doctorate in medicine in 1858, and in 1859 he was sent abroad for three years, most of them in Heidelberg, where he worked in Erlenmeyer’s laboratory with Mendeleev among his colleagues. In Heidelberg in 1861 he met the pianist Ekaterina Protopopova, who played Schumann and Chopin to him. They married after his return to Saint Petersburg in 1862.
